questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.stem: Demand is more elastic than supply. Who bears more of a tax?

options.text: Sellers bear more because supply is less elastic.
Buyers bear more because demand is elastic.
Both bear equal shares.
The government bears it all.

questions.explanation: The less elastic side bears more. Supply is less elastic, so sellers bear more.
questions.hint: Less elastic means more burden.

questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.stem: Explain why a binding price floor can waste resources.

answer.exemplar: A binding floor creates surplus units that are produced but not bought, wasting labor and materials on unneeded output.

questions.explanation: Surplus output uses resources that could serve other needs. Waste follows.
questions.hint: Surplus units still cost resources.

questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.stem: Explain why a binding price ceiling causes non-price rationing.

answer.exemplar: With price fixed below equilibrium, quantity demanded exceeds supply, so sellers ration by queues, favoritism, or black markets.

questions.explanation: Price cannot rise, so other mechanisms allocate scarce seats.
questions.hint: Price cannot clear the market.

questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.stem: Transit rides are a normal good. What happens to demand when incomes rise?

options.text: Demand shifts left as riders buy cars.
Demand is unchanged because price is fixed.
Demand shifts right as riders spend more.
Supply shifts right to meet demand.

questions.explanation: For a normal good, higher income raises demand, shifting right.
questions.hint: Normal good means demand rises with income.

questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: Predict equilibrium after demand and supply both shift right
questions.stem: Demand and supply both shift right. What is certain about price?

options.text: Price must rise.
Price must fall.
Price is unchanged.
Price direction is indeterminate.

questions.explanation: Both shifts raise quantity, but price direction depends on relative magnitudes.
questions.hint: Price is not determined here.

questions.subject: MICROECONOMICS
questions.stem: Explain why a price rise in one good can raise demand for another.

answer.exemplar: If two goods are substitutes, a higher price in one pushes consumers toward the other, raising its demand.

questions.explanation: Substitutes replace each other, so a price rise in one shifts demand to the other.
questions.hint: Substitutes replace each other.
